extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (Aristotle / virtue ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a classical ethics treatise setting out evaluative standards for character traits (e.g., jocularity, shame, reserve) and for kinds of justice (distributive, corrective, reciprocity) with definitions, examples, and procedural implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration / Exaggerator (vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who pretend to qualities with a view to gain and exaggerate their attributes (e.g., claiming skills like soothsaying or medicine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as a vice opposed to the Truthful Man; people who pretend to abilities that neighbours can avail themselves of are common and despicable. Exaggeration arises from aiming at gain; it is morally censurable because it misrepresents and seeks advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve (depreciating one's own qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depreciating one's own qualities so as to avoid appearing to speak for gain; often gives the appearance of refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate reserve (especially when truth is not obvious) gives an impression of refinement and is often associated with denying common opinions (Socratic trait). But extreme reserve can resemble exaggeration or other excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factotum (false claim to small obvious things)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who falsely lay claim to small things whose falsity is obvious are called Factotums and are very despicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern: claiming trivial or blatantly false accomplishments undermines character and is socially condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jocularity / Tact (the mean concerning jesting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state in joking: to say and listen to things fit for a good man and a gentleman — the jocularity of good taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by saying what is becoming, avoiding to pain the object of wit, and sometimes giving him pleasure; includes the capacity to hear what one says. Distinguishes gentlemanly jocularity from vulgar or uneducated varieties (e.g., Old Comedy's obscenity vs New Comedy's innuendo). The refined man is a 'law to himself' about permissible jesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffoon (excess in jocularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who exceed in the ridiculous, catching at it in any way and aiming at laughter rather than what is fitting; spare neither themselves nor others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buffoons prioritize laughs over decency and avoiding harm; their jocularity is 'easy pleasantry' but lacks refinement. Anti-pattern: using obscene or hurtful material just to elicit laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clownish / Stern (defect in jocularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who would not for the world make a joke themselves and are displeased with such as do; contribute nothing jocose and are savage toward jokers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defect of jocularity: lack of ease or social poise in light-hearted exchange, making a person socially useless in playful intercourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bearing and hearing of jest (reciprocal tolerance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man will say such things as he will bear to hear; the capacity to both utter and tolerate appropriate jests is part of tact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits apply: some scurrility is legally or socially forbidden. A gentleman will regulate his own jesting according to what he can tolerate in hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shame (pathic feeling vs virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shame is a feeling ('a kind of fear of disgrace') rather than a moral state; appropriate chiefly to youth as a check on passion-driven wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shame produces physical effects (blushing) and is praised in the young but not in the old (a good man ought not to need shame because he does not voluntarily do disgraceful acts). Thus shame is not properly a virtue; it may be useful only insofar as it prevents wrong in those still learning self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control (mixed state)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-control is described as not properly a virtue but a kind of mixed state (full account deferred to later discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flagged for future detailed treatment; indicates nuance in classifying moral states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a moral state enabling just action and desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is a moral state such that, in consequence of it, people have the capacity of doing what is just and actually do it, and wish it; the counterpart holds for Injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the broad defining criterion: justice is a dispositional moral excellence related to action toward others, not merely one-off acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness as a sense of Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who act according to law are called Just, and violators of law Unjust; laws aim at common good or the good of the best, and lawful things are in a manner Just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law commands conduct across virtues (bravery, temperance, meekness); a good law directs toward common happiness. This connects legal conformity with moral justness, though different senses of 'just' exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as perfect virtue toward one's neighbour
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is 'perfect Virtue' insofar as it is exercised toward one's neighbour; it makes virtue 'a good to others' because it benefits other persons, not merely oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why justice is often seen as the highest virtue: it requires applying virtue in social relations and in dealings with others (e.g., rulers, fellow-subjects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Justice (distinct part of virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a particular Justice that is a part of Virtue (not co-extensive with all of Virtue); this is the species concerned with distributions and corrective transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between Justice as whole/co-extensive with Virtue and the narrower particular justice that governs interactions, exchanges, and distributions among people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of Particular Justice: Distributive and Corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular Justice includes (1) distribution of honour, wealth, etc. (distributive justice) and (2) corrective justice arising in transactions between people (corrective justice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective transactions are further divided into voluntary (selling, buying, hiring, bail, borrowing, deposit) and involuntary (theft, poisoning, assault, false witness) categories; the appropriate form of justice differs by type of transaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive Justice = proportionate equality (geometrical proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributive Justice is proportionate: shares should be assigned according to some rate (A:B::C:D), so that persons receive shares in proportion to the relevant merit or criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'rate' may be contested (democrats: freedom, oligarchs: wealth, aristocrats: virtue); distributive justice is a mean, a geometrical proportion preserving ratios between persons and things. Example: joining first and third, second and fourth proportionals preserves the just distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective Justice = arithmetic equality (mean between gain and loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrective Justice aims to restore equality between the parties after an unequal transaction by making the mean between loss and gain (judge takes from the greater and gives to the less).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes the judge seeks to make parties have their own (no loss, no gain). The corrective is arithmetical: restore the pre-transaction equality through compensation or penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing gain/loss and the judge's role
rubrics_metrics.description: In corrective contexts, actions create gain and loss (having more = gain; having less = loss); the judge's office is to make things equal again, acting as the personification of the Just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge is a 'middle-man' aiming at the mean; practical rule: take from the greater the excess over the mean and add it to the less. This is applied irrespective of moral quality of parties (the law looks to difference created by injury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs involuntary transactions (relevance to justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transactions are classed as voluntary (originate voluntarily: selling, buying, hiring, etc.) or involuntary (theft, assassination, secret crimes); this distinction affects how justice is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice in voluntary exchanges is handled differently (e.g., exchanges governed by proportion and commensuration) than in involuntary wrongs (where corrective justice and legal penalty operate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocation must be proportionate (not strict equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocation as a principle of justice only fits when it is proportionate, not simple mirror retaliation or exact equality; reciprocation according to proportion binds exchanges and social bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: one in authority should not be struck in turn; reward and requital should be proportionate. For exchange, reciprocation requires prior equalization (quality/quantity) of goods so that proportionate returns are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensuration and money as measure (practical tool for distributive justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: All things that can be exchanged must be comparable; money serves as a common measure (νόμισμα) representing Demand and making diverse goods commensurable for proportionate exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money equalizes by measuring and setting prices so exchanges can be made at any time; it approximates equality across qualitatively different goods for practical purposes and thus enables proportionate reciprocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice aims at the mean; Injustice occupies extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Just action is the mean between acting unjustly (taking more) and being acted unjustly upon (receiving less); Injustice aims at producing excess or defect (both extremes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral description: Justice as mean-state aims to produce proportion; Injustice violates proportion and thus both extremes. This conceptual frame underlies the other technical criteria for distributive and corrective justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Justice requires mutual law and possibility of injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Social (communal) justice presupposes mutually acknowledged law and the possibility of injustice (adjudication distinguishes Just from Unjust); those outside such mutual arrangements lack the same Social Just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: justice in social relations depends on shared legal/communal structures; governance should be by principle rather than by a single man, since a ruler governs for self otherwise and threatens equality.
